q: Which four top-level sections are most commonly used in an ARM template?
exp: An ARM template's main sections are parameters (values you pass in), variables (values worked out inside the template), resources (what to deploy) and outputs (values returned afterwards). There are also $schema, contentVersion and optional functions. The other sets of names aren't template sections.

q: What is the difference between a parameter and a variable in an ARM template?
opts: Parameters accept values at deployment time; variables are computed inside the template
Variables accept values at deployment time; parameters are computed inside the template
exp: Parameters are the inputs of a template: you supply their values at deployment time (on the command line or in a parameter file), so the same template works for dev and prod. Variables are values the template calculates for itself, often from parameters, and the person deploying can't set them. Both can have types, and parameters aren't only for passwords.

q: You deploy a template to a resource group in Complete mode. The RG contains a VM that isn't in the template. What happens?
exp: In Complete mode, Resource Manager makes the resource group match the template exactly, so any resource in the group that the template doesn't define — like this VM — is deleted. In the default Incremental mode, resources not in the template are left untouched. That's why Complete mode is risky and rarely used.

q: What is the default ARM deployment mode?
exp: Incremental is the default: resources in the template are created or updated, and everything else in the resource group is left alone. Complete mode deletes resources not in the template. 'Validate' only checks a template without deploying, and 'Overwrite' isn't a mode.

q: Before deploying a modified template to production, you want to preview exactly which resources would change. Use:
exp: The what-if operation (az deployment group what-if, or create --confirm-with-what-if) compares the template with what's currently deployed and lists every resource that would be created, modified or deleted — without changing anything. The Activity log shows past operations, Advisor gives recommendations, and az group delete has no dry-run.

q: Which CLI command deploys a template file to a resource group?
opts: az deployment group create --resource-group RG1 --template-file azuredeploy.json
exp: az deployment group create deploys a template (JSON or Bicep) into a resource group, with --resource-group and --template-file (plus parameters). The PowerShell equivalent is New-AzResourceGroupDeployment. Use az deployment sub create for subscription scope. The other commands don't exist.

q: You configured a VM in the portal and want a template of it to redeploy later. Quickest built-in option?
opts: Use Export template on the resource or resource group
Use Azure Policy to export the resource's definition
exp: Export template (on a resource or resource group in the portal) generates an ARM JSON template from what's deployed, which you can save and redeploy. Expect to clean it up, for example by turning hard-coded values into parameters. Azure Policy doesn't produce templates.

q: Which statement about Bicep is TRUE?
opts: Bicep deploys through a separate engine from ARM
Bicep transpiles to ARM JSON, so anything ARM templates can deploy, Bicep can too
Bicep supports only VMs and networks, so other resources still need separate ARM templates
Bicep files must be converted manually before every deployment
exp: Bicep is a simpler language for ARM templates. When you deploy, it's compiled (transpiled) into ARM JSON and Resource Manager deploys it in the usual way. That means every resource type and API version available in ARM is available in Bicep, and the Azure CLI and PowerShell compile Bicep automatically.

q: Which command converts an existing ARM JSON template into a Bicep file?
exp: az bicep decompile --file azuredeploy.json converts an ARM JSON template into a .bicep file (you may need to tidy it afterwards). az bicep build does the reverse, turning Bicep into ARM JSON. az bicep export isn't a command.

q: In Bicep, how do you reference the name of a resource declared as resource stg 'Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts@2023-01-01' = {...}?
exp: In Bicep each resource has a symbolic name (here stg), and you use it directly to read properties: stg.name, stg.id or stg.properties.primaryEndpoints. This also creates the deployment dependency automatically. reference() and the square-bracket syntax are ARM JSON.

q: In ARM JSON, "[parameters('location')]" is an example of:
opts: A template expression calling a template function
A variable declaration with a default value
exp: In ARM JSON, a string that starts with [ and ends with ] is a template expression that's evaluated at deployment. Inside it, parameters('location') is a template function that returns the value of the 'location' parameter. Comments use // and variables are declared in the variables section.

q: Answer Yes or No:
stmts: Complete mode is supported only for resource group deployments
A template can deploy to more than one resource group using nested/linked deployments
secureString parameter values are logged in deployment history
Bicep supports modules for reusing code
exp: Complete mode only works for resource group deployments. A template can deploy to other resource groups through nested or linked deployments. Values of secureString parameters are never logged in deployment history. Bicep supports modules for reusing code.

q: What SLA applies to two or more VMs deployed across two or more availability zones in the same region?
exp: Spreading two or more VMs across two or more availability zones gives a 99.99% VM connectivity SLA, because each zone is a separate datacenter with its own power and networking. Two or more VMs in an availability set give 99.95%, and a single VM with Premium SSD or Ultra disks gives 99.9%.

q: An availability set protects against:
opts: Rack failures and planned maintenance reboots within a datacenter
Failure of a whole availability zone within the same Azure region
exp: An availability set spreads VMs across fault domains (separate racks with their own power and network) and update domains (groups rebooted one at a time during planned maintenance). It protects against hardware and maintenance events inside one datacenter, but not a whole zone or region failing, and not someone deleting a VM.

q: What are the maximum fault domains and update domains you can configure in an availability set?
exp: An availability set supports up to 3 fault domains (some regions allow only 2) and up to 20 update domains (5 by default). The other combinations aren't valid limits.

q: VM1 was deployed without an availability set. You now want it in AVSet1. What must you do?
opts: Stop (deallocate) the VM and edit its availability settings
Delete and recreate the VM (keeping disks and NIC)
Move it with az vm update
exp: A VM's availability set can only be chosen when the VM is created. To add an existing VM, delete it while keeping its disks and NIC, then create a new VM from those disks with the availability set specified. There's no setting, az vm update option or restart that changes it.

q: Which managed disk type gives the highest performance, with configurable IOPS and throughput?
exp: Ultra Disk offers the highest performance and lets you set IOPS and throughput independently of disk size, even while the VM is running. Premium SSD is fast but its performance is tied to its size tier. Standard SSD and Standard HDD are cheaper and slower.

q: A single VM (no availability set or zone) must qualify for a 99.9% SLA. What's required?
opts: Premium SSD (or Ultra) for all OS and data disks
Standard SSD disks with accelerated networking enabled
exp: A single VM (not in an availability set or zone) gets the 99.9% SLA only if every OS and data disk is Premium SSD, Premium SSD v2 or Ultra Disk. With Standard SSD or HDD, the single-instance SLA is lower. Accelerated networking doesn't affect the SLA.

q: Azure Disk Encryption uses which technologies on Windows and Linux respectively?
exp: Azure Disk Encryption works inside the VM: on Windows it uses BitLocker and on Linux it uses dm-crypt, with keys stored in Azure Key Vault. SSE is the platform encryption done by the storage service, TDE is for SQL databases, and Always Encrypted is a SQL feature.

q: Azure Disk Encryption requires which supporting resource, with which constraint?
opts: A storage account with geo-redundancy in the region paired with the VM
A key vault in the same region and subscription as the VM
exp: Azure Disk Encryption stores its keys and secrets in Azure Key Vault. The vault must be in the same region and subscription as the VM, and its access policy must have 'Azure Disk Encryption for volume encryption' enabled. Storage accounts, Log Analytics and on-premises HSMs aren't used for this.

q: How does encryption at host differ from Azure Disk Encryption?
opts: It encrypts data on the VM host itself, with no agent or extension inside the VM
It encrypts only the OS disk with BitLocker and stores the keys in the guest registry
It works only with unmanaged disks
exp: Encryption at host encrypts data on the physical host that runs the VM — including temp disks and OS and data disk caches — before it reaches storage. Nothing runs inside the VM. Azure Disk Encryption, by contrast, runs BitLocker or dm-crypt inside the guest OS. Encryption at host works for Windows and Linux with managed disks.

q: You resize a VM to a size that isn't available on its current hardware cluster. What's required?
opts: Deallocate the VM first, then resize
exp: Each VM runs on a hardware cluster that supports a set of sizes. If the new size isn't on the current cluster, Azure must move the VM to different hardware, so you have to stop (deallocate) it first and then resize. Deleting the VM or changing subscription isn't needed.

q: You must move a VM to a different region. Supported approach?
opts: Change the region in the VM properties
Use Azure Resource Mover (or Site Recovery) to replicate and move it
Export the template and change only the location; disks move automatically
exp: A VM's region can't be changed. Azure Resource Mover (or Azure Site Recovery) replicates the VM and its dependent resources to the target region and then completes the move. There's no region setting or move command, and exporting a template doesn't copy disks.

q: Which statement about moving a VM to another resource group or subscription is true?
opts: The VM must be deleted first
Only stopped VMs, via a support ticket
exp: You can move a VM to another resource group or subscription without deleting it, but its dependent resources (disks, NIC, public IP and sometimes the VNet) must move with it. The resource ID changes because it contains the resource group name. The region stays the same.

q: Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets are mainly used to:
opts: Deploy and automatically scale a set of VMs based on demand
Encrypt and patch a set of VMs from one central policy
exp: A virtual machine scale set deploys and manages a group of VMs created from the same configuration, and adds or removes instances automatically based on demand (autoscale). It isn't a backup, encryption or monitoring service, although it works with all of those.

q: An autoscale rule says: if average CPU > 75% for 10 minutes, add 2 instances; maximum 10. There are 9 instances now, and CPU has been 80% for 15 minutes. What happens?
exp: Autoscale never goes above the maximum instance count. The rule says add 2, but with 9 running and a maximum of 10 only 1 instance can be added, so the scale set ends up with 10. It doesn't stop or disable itself.

q: Which scale set orchestration mode lets you mix manually created VMs with scale-set instances of different VM types?
exp: Flexible orchestration lets a scale set contain VMs of different sizes and include standard VMs you created separately, and spreads them across fault domains. Uniform orchestration uses identical instances from one model. Classic and Hybrid aren't orchestration modes.

q: Which CLI command creates a Linux VM and generates SSH keys automatically?
opts: az vm create -g RG1 -n VM1 --image Ubuntu2204 --generate-ssh-keys
az compute vm create -g RG1 -n VM1 --os linux --ssh auto-generate
exp: az vm create creates a VM. --image Ubuntu2204 picks Linux, and --generate-ssh-keys creates an SSH key pair in ~/.ssh if none exists and puts the public key on the VM. New-AzVM is PowerShell and has no -Linux switch, and the other commands don't exist.

q: Answer Yes or No:
stmts: A Standard SKU public IP keeps the same address when its VM is deallocated and started again
A VM can be added to an availability zone after creation without recreating it
Spot VMs can be evicted when Azure needs the capacity back
Resizing a VM in an availability set may require deallocating ALL VMs in the set
exp: Standard public IPs are always static, so the address survives deallocation (Basic SKU dynamic IPs were retired in September 2025). Zone placement is set at creation; Spot VMs are evictable; resizing to new hardware in an availability set may require stopping all VMs in the set.

q: Order the steps to encrypt a VM's disks with ADE using a key encryption key (KEK):
items: Run Set-AzVMDiskEncryptionExtension referencing the vault and KEK
Create a key vault with enabled-for-disk-encryption
Create the KEK in the vault
Create or identify the target VM
exp: First create the key vault with 'enabled for disk encryption', because the encryption extension stores secrets there. Then create the key encryption key (KEK) in that vault. With the target VM ready, run Set-AzVMDiskEncryptionExtension, pointing at the vault and KEK, to turn on BitLocker or dm-crypt.

q: Which Azure Container Registry SKU supports geo-replication?
exp: Geo-replication, which keeps a copy of the registry in several regions behind one name, is available only in the Premium SKU of Azure Container Registry. Premium also adds private endpoints and higher throughput. Basic and Standard are single-region.

q: Which command builds an image in the cloud (no local Docker) and pushes it to the registry in one step?
exp: az acr build sends your source code and Dockerfile to Azure Container Registry, which builds the image in the cloud (an ACR Task) and pushes it to the registry, so you don't need Docker installed locally. docker push needs a locally built image, az acr import copies an existing image, and az container create runs a container.

q: An app must pull images from ACR without storing credentials. Best practice:
opts: Enable the admin account and put the password in code
Use a managed identity with the AcrPull role on the registry
exp: Give the app a managed identity and assign it the AcrPull role on the registry. The app then authenticates with Microsoft Entra ID, so no password is stored anywhere, and it can pull but not push. The admin account is a shared password, and anonymous pull makes images public.

q: Azure Container Instances is best suited for:
opts: Long-running fleets of orchestrated microservices that need a service mesh and rolling upgrades
Fast, serverless, per-second-billed single containers or small container groups
exp: Azure Container Instances runs a container (or a small group of containers) in seconds without managing VMs or an orchestrator, and bills per second while it runs. That suits short tasks, batch jobs and simple apps. Large fleets of microservices with scaling and service discovery need Container Apps or AKS.

q: In an ACI container group, the containers:
opts: Run on separate hosts, each with its own IP address, and can't share any volumes
Share a host, lifecycle, and local network (localhost), and can share volumes
exp: Containers in one ACI container group are scheduled on the same host and share a lifecycle, a network (they reach each other on localhost and share one IP) and optionally storage volumes — like a pod in Kubernetes. They can communicate, and mixing operating systems in one group isn't supported.

q: Which restart policy makes an ACI container run once like a batch job?
exp: With the Never restart policy, ACI runs the container once and leaves it stopped when it exits; with OnFailure, it restarts it only if it fails. Both suit batch jobs, and you stop paying once it has finished. Always keeps restarting the container, which is meant for long-running services.

q: Which capability does Azure Container Apps have that ACI doesn't?
opts: Built-in autoscaling (including to zero), revisions, and traffic splitting
Public IP addresses, DNS name labels, and mounted Azure Files volumes
exp: Azure Container Apps adds features that ACI doesn't have: automatic scaling (including scaling to zero) driven by KEDA rules on HTTP traffic, queues and events; revisions; and splitting traffic between revisions. Both services can run Linux containers, use public IPs and set environment variables.

q: An event-driven container app should run zero instances when the queue is empty and scale out as messages arrive. Configure:
opts: Minimum replicas = 0 with a KEDA queue-based scale rule
Minimum replicas = 1 with manual scaling from the portal
exp: Set the minimum replica count to 0 and add a KEDA scale rule based on the queue length (for example an Azure Storage Queue or Service Bus rule). When the queue is empty the app runs no replicas and costs nothing; as messages arrive, Container Apps adds replicas. Always-on or manual scaling would keep instances running.

q: You need to run a Windows container for a short task with the least management overhead. Choose:
exp: Azure Container Instances can run a Windows container on demand without any cluster or VM to manage, and you pay per second until the task finishes. AKS and VMSS need much more setup and management, and the App Service Free tier isn't meant for running containers like this.

q: Answer Yes or No:
stmts: All ACR SKUs store Docker/OCI images
A multi-container ACI group is Linux-only
Container Apps runs on Kubernetes but doesn't expose the Kubernetes API
ACI containers can mount Azure file shares as volumes
exp: All four are true. Every ACR SKU stores Docker and OCI images (SKUs differ in throughput and features). Multi-container groups in ACI are supported only for Linux. Container Apps runs on Kubernetes that Microsoft manages, so you never use the Kubernetes API yourself. ACI can mount an Azure file share as a volume for persistent data.

q: An App Service plan determines:
opts: The app's name, its custom domain, and its deployment credentials
The region, instance size, and features available to all apps in the plan
exp: An App Service plan defines the compute your apps run on: the region, the operating system, the pricing tier (which features are available) and the instance size and count. Every app in the plan shares those instances. The app name, DNS zone and storage pricing are set elsewhere.

q: Which is the lowest tier that supports deployment slots and scheduled backups?
exp: Deployment slots start at Standard (5 slots), so Standard is the lowest tier with both. Backups alone are available from Basic: automatic hourly backups plus custom scheduled backups to a storage account (Basic can back up only the production slot).

q: What's the difference between scaling up and scaling out an App Service plan?
opts: Up = more instances of the same size; Out = a more powerful tier or size
Up = a more powerful tier or size; Out = more instances of the same size
exp: Scaling up means moving to a bigger instance size or a higher pricing tier (more CPU, memory or features). Scaling out means adding more instances of the same size so load is spread across them. Both apply to App Service plans.

q: Rule-based autoscale for App Service requires at least which tier?
exp: Rule-based autoscale (for example, add an instance when CPU is above 70%) is available from the Standard tier. Basic supports scaling out only manually, and Free and Shared can't scale out at all. Isolated also supports autoscale, but it isn't the minimum.

q: What's the main benefit of swapping a staging slot into production instead of redeploying?
opts: Cheaper compute, because the staging slot stops after each swap
Near-zero downtime with pre-warmed instances and an easy swap back
exp: When you swap a staging slot into production, App Service first warms up the new version on the production instances, then switches traffic over, so users see almost no downtime. If something goes wrong, you swap back immediately. Swapping doesn't cut costs, review code or provide certificates.

q: During a swap, which settings stay with their slot instead of following the app content?
opts: App settings and connection strings marked as deployment slot settings
Custom domain names, TLS certificates, and all app settings swap
The code stays; settings always swap
exp: App settings and connection strings marked 'Deployment slot setting' are sticky: they stay with their slot when you swap. That's how production keeps its own database connection string while new code moves in. Settings without that mark move with the app. TLS certificates aren't the only slot-specific item.

q: To map www.contoso.com to an App Service app, which DNS records do you create?
opts: A CNAME to the app's azurewebsites.net hostname, plus a TXT asuid verification record
An SRV record for port 443, plus an MX record that points to the app's IP
exp: For a subdomain such as www, create a CNAME record that points to the app's default host name (<app>.azurewebsites.net), plus a TXT record named asuid.www containing the app's domain verification ID, which proves you own the domain. MX is for email, SRV for services and NS for delegation. Apex domains use an A record instead.

q: Which statement about free App Service managed certificates is TRUE?
opts: They support wildcard domains and can be exported as a PFX, but must be renewed by hand every year
They cover custom domains with auto-renewal, but don't support wildcards and can't be exported
They must be bought from a CA
They work on the Free tier
exp: Free App Service managed certificates secure custom domains such as www.contoso.com and renew automatically. They don't support wildcard domains (*.contoso.com), can't be exported, and need the Basic tier or higher — not Free. You don't buy them from a certificate authority.

q: An App Service app must call a database on a private IP in your VNet. Which feature?
opts: A private endpoint on the app (inbound)
exp: Regional VNet integration gives an App Service app outbound access into a virtual network, so it can call a database on a private IP. A private endpoint does the opposite: it gives clients in the VNet private inbound access to the app. Access restrictions filter inbound traffic, and Hybrid Connections reach individual hosts through a relay.

ctx: A production web app runs on plan S1 with 1 instance. Requirements: deploy without downtime, scale on CPU up to 5 instances, allow browsing only from the office IP, back up nightly.
q: Answer Yes or No:
stmts: Deployment slots meet the no-downtime requirement on S1
S1 supports CPU-based autoscale to 5 instances
Office-only access is configured with Access restrictions
exp: All four are true on S1 (Standard). Standard includes deployment slots, so you can deploy to staging and swap with no downtime. It supports rule-based autoscale up to 10 instances, so 5 is fine. Access restrictions limit inbound traffic to the office IP. Standard also supports scheduled custom backups (available from Basic).
